title: Ministry of Defence 2025-26 (departmental overview)
date_evidence: OVERVIEW Ministry of Defence 2025-26 September 2026 (PDF title page); NAO overview page for the same document shows 15 Sep 2026, modified 2026-09-15T10:05:30+00:00
key_claim: Total departmental spending is projected to rise 18% from 62 billion to 73.3 billion pounds by 2029-30, capital rising to 44% of the total; the plan's delay from autumn 2025 to June 2026 has led some small businesses to exit the defence sector.
frame_summary: The NAO treats the Defence Investment Plan as a signal to industry whose delay already imposed costs on small suppliers, specialist skills and investment, while spending growth itself is real and capital-heavy.
verbatim_quote: However, continued uncertainty, including over some procurement processes, has led some small businesses to exit the defence sector, resulted in the loss of specialist skills, increased costs for critical components, and potentially affected investment in the UK defence industry.
verbatim_list: Total DEL spending is projected to increase by 18% (from £62 billion to £73.3 billion)
Capital spending is expected to account for 44% of total DEL by 2029-30, up from 28% in 2020-21.
However, its publication was delayed from autumn 2025 until June 2026.

title: Initial response to the Defence Investment Plan
date_evidence: Published on 30 June 2026 (page text; no published_time meta tag)
key_claim: Planned NATO-qualifying spending is 2.6% of GDP in 2026-27 and 2.7% in 2027-28 and 2028-29, about 3.8 billion pounds a year extra, just over a third of the way to 3.5%; around a third of the increase was unfunded and reaching 3.5% needs about 25 billion pounds a year more by 2035.
frame_summary: The IFS argues the plan buys only a small step toward the 3.5% pledge, leaves a third of the uplift unfunded and defers the hard fiscal choice to the Budget and beyond.

publisher: International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS)
title: NATO's New Defence Spending Target: Who's planning What in 2026?
key_claim: Sixteen NATO Allies, the UK among them, are in the baseline group aiming for 5% by 2035, and few of them have developed or published a roadmap for financing the increase.
frame_summary: ICDS sorts Allies by how credibly they plan to reach the 3.5% core target and finds the largest group, which includes the UK, has the target but not a published financing path.
verbatim_quote: However, few of these Allies have developed, or at least made public, a roadmap describing how they intend to finance their increasing defence budgets.
verbatim_list: The third group, the ‘baseline Allies’, is by far the largest (16 Allies)
The UK, for example, faces difficult choices if it is to finance defence spending at the required level.

title: Defence Spending Must Become Defence Capacity
date_evidence: 13 July 2026 (guest commentary by Ian Ball, John Crompton and Dag Detter)
key_claim: RUSI commentators ask whether the target should be 2.5%, 2.7%, 3% or 3.5% of GDP and argue the harder test is whether spending becomes readiness.
frame_summary: The authors argue the plan shows where money may go but Parliament cannot yet see whether spending, assets and maintenance become usable capacity.
verbatim_quote: The harder test is whether ministers can show how spending, assets, maintenance and liabilities become readiness.

title: UK to set 3% defence spending date in spring review
key_claim: The 3% date is to be set at a spring 2027 spending review; core NATO spending is 2.7% of GDP from 2027/28 through 2029/30; the remaining 4.7 billion pounds of plan funding is to be identified at Budget 2026 on 28 October.
frame_summary: Frames the chancellor's promise as a dated route still to come: the funded trajectory is flat at 2.7% and the 3% date, and the missing 4.7 billion pounds, are decisions for later events.

title: Prime Minister considers delaying decision on UK defence spending, according to reports
key_claim: Reports on 6 October said the defence Spending Review could move from spring to autumn 2027, with an October 2027 working assumption; a Treasury spokesperson called the reports pure rumour and speculation.
frame_summary: The ADS trade site relays the reported delay as a concern for firms waiting for clarity on procurement, while recording the Treasury denial.
